title: Montana Governor Lands in India to Rescue Lentil Exports Amid MAGA Backlash
excerpt: Governor Greg Gianforte is leading a 30-member delegation to India and Sri Lanka to rebuild the state's collapsed pulse trade, even as anti-India voices in his own party attack the trip.
body:
• Montana Governor Greg Gianforte is leading a 30-plus member delegation to India and Sri Lanka, with trade, agriculture, critical minerals, biotech, and university partnerships on the agenda.
  • Reviving pulse exports is the centerpiece: Montana's lentil shipments to India collapsed from $64 million to $14 million last year, and the governor is pressing for "long-term relationships" with consistent buying.
  • The trip has drawn fire from MAGA-aligned online voices, including calls for Gianforte's impeachment, accusing the Republican governor of courting India despite protectionist "Montana First" sentiment.
  • What it means for you: US senators want "favorable pulse crop provisions" in the US-India trade deal — a breakthrough could ease the duties squeezing both Montana farmers and Indian buyers of American daal.

Opening lead

Montana Governor Greg Gianforte arrived in India this week with more than 30 farmers, university presidents, and biotech executives in tow — on a mission to sell American lentils to the world's biggest daal-eating nation, even as voices in his own party's base say the trip should never have happened.

https://x.com/USAmbIndia/status/2107075722690924905

The week-long delegation, which also visits Sri Lanka, will meet ministerial leaders and partners across trade, agriculture, bioscience, photonics, quantum, energy, and education, according to the governor's office. But the emotional core of the visit is pulses — lentils, peas, and chickpeas — the crop Montana grows more of than any other US state.

Context & Background

India is the world's largest consumer of pulses, and for years it was a major buyer of Montana's harvest. That trade has cratered: Montana's lentil exports to India fell from $64 million to $14 million last year, a collapse of nearly 78 percent. Indian duties on American pulses — combined with cheaper supplies from Canada and elsewhere — priced Montana growers out.

US politicians have been pressing the issue for months. In February, Senator Steve Daines traveled to India to advocate for Montana's pulse farmers, meeting Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal in New Delhi and vowing to push for "favorable pulse crop provisions" in any US-India trade agreement, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Daines and Senator Kevin Cramer also wrote to President Donald Trump asking for tariff relief for American pulse growers, who they said had lost market share to Canada. Agriculture remains one of the most sensitive chapters of the ongoing US-India bilateral trade negotiations, with New Delhi guarding its farmers and Washington demanding market access.

Gianforte, who also chairs the Republican Governors Association, has framed the mission as reciprocal. "Well, it's important that we have long-term relationships. This is why I wanted to bring our pulse crop growers with me," he said in Delhi. "We would like to have long-term relationships where, as we continue to buy Indian products and import them into the US, we need consistent markets here as well, because we have delicious lentils."

Impact & Analysis

The backlash at home has been fierce. MAGA-aligned social media accounts attacked the governor for speaking of technology partnerships and Indian students in the same breath as trade. "He should be impeached," one widely shared post read. "Montana has literally nothing to gain from India. India possesses NOTHING that Montana needs," wrote another. A Montana conservative blog demanded "MONTANA FIRST," questioning what the state gains when the agenda includes critical minerals, manufacturing technology, and university research rather than finished Montana-made products.

The episode captures a real tension inside the Republican coalition: heartland farm economies need export markets, while the party's populist wing treats engagement with India as a threat to American workers. Some of the angriest commentary targeted not lentils but people: Indian tech workers and students, with "university partnerships" read as a pipeline for foreign nationals.

"We would like to have long-term relationships where, as we continue to buy Indian products and import them into the US, we need consistent markets here as well, because we have delicious lentils."

— Greg Gianforte, Governor of Montana

Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, the trip is a study in contrasts: a Republican governor lands in Delhi praising Indian students — Montana "loves" having them, his team noted — even as anti-India voices online demand his impeachment for the outreach. The economic reality is simpler: Indian consumers are among the world's biggest buyers of exactly what Montana grows, and the delegation's university and biotech agenda could open research and exchange slots that benefit Indian students. Indian grocery stores across the US, which stock Montana-origin lentils and peas, also have a quiet stake in whether this trade recovers.

What's Next

The delegation continues to Sri Lanka after its India leg. The real test comes in the negotiating room: whether the US-India bilateral trade talks, now grinding through agriculture's sensitivities, produce the pulse-tariff relief Montana's senators have demanded. If they do, Montana's $14 million export figure has far to climb — and Indian kitchens get steadier American daal supplies.
